title: How Impeachment Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how impeachment works, prompted by a suggestion from Josh's father-in-law Steve. They cover the British origins in fourteenth-century Parliament, the drafting of the US Constitution's impeachment clause (the "high crimes and misdemeanors" wording, George Mason's "maladministration" and Ben Franklin's remarks), and how the House (simple majority) and Senate (two-thirds) process works, including managers acting as prosecutors. Case histories include Andrew Johnson's 1868 trial (Edmund Ross's single deciding vote and the Tenure of Office Act), Nixon's Watergate-era articles and resignation, Clinton's 1998-99 impeachment and acquittal, and the impeachment of federal judges and Senator William Blount. The episode closes with discussion of 2017 impeachment talk around Donald Trump and a listener mail segment on red velvet cake and banana bread.

entities.name: Impeached: The Trial of Andrew Johnson and the Fight for Lincoln's Legacy

segments.title: Opening banter and Steve's suggestion
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the show, Josh credits his father-in-law Steve with suggesting an episode on impeachment, and they tease the topic's relevance to current events.

segments.title: Andrew Johnson's 1868 impeachment
segments.summary: The hosts describe Andrew Johnson's clash with Republicans over Reconstruction, his veto of civil rights legislation, and the Tenure of Office Act, which led to his impeachment after he fired Edwin Stanton. They describe Senator Edmund Ross's single deciding vote to acquit.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Podcast break before the next section.

segments.title: Origins in British Parliament and the word impeachment
segments.summary: The hosts trace the Latin and French roots of impeach, then describe the fourteenth-century English origins where the House of Commons began impeaching royal appointees such as Roger Mortimer and Chief Justice Willoughby.

segments.title: Drafting the Constitution's impeachment clause
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how the framers added brief impeachment language, the debate over George Mason's maladministration wording, the adoption of bribery, treason, and high crimes and misdemeanors, and how the phrase is interpreted today.

segments.title: The House and Senate impeachment process
segments.summary: The hosts explain that articles of impeachment can be introduced by any representative, that the House needs a simple majority, and that the Senate needs a two-thirds vote to convict, with House members serving as managers who act as prosecutors. Josh's uncle Ed Bryan served as a manager in the Clinton trial.

segments.title: Nixon, Watergate, and Clinton impeachments
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Nixon's resignation during Watergate and its articles of impeachment, then Clinton's 1998 impeachment for perjury and obstruction tied to Monica Lewinsky, and the close party-line Senate vote that acquitted him.

segments.title: Federal judges, Senator Blount, and Trump impeachment talk
segments.summary: The hosts note that federal judges have been the most often convicted officials, that Senator William Blount's case established senators cannot be impeached, and they discuss talk of impeaching Donald Trump and the House Judiciary Committee leadership race.

segments.title: Wrap-up
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck close the main discussion, suggest listeners search the topic online, and move to listener mail.

segments.title: Listener mail: red velvet cake and banana bread
segments.summary: A listener follow-up on the cake episode explains that red velvet cake's color came from a cocoa, vinegar, and buttermilk reaction that no longer works with modern cocoa, and that very ripe bananas add sweetness to banana bread.
